claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental analysis of endogenous PCM proteins in C. elegans as described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: SPD-5 and γ-TuRC occupy distinct regions from known binding partners SPD-2 and MZT-1, respectively.
claims.source: We find that C. elegans PCM is composed of overlapping spheres of proteins similar to what has been observed in other systems, with SPD-5 and γ-TuRC occupying distinct regions from known binding partners SPD-2 and MZT-1, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental analysis of endogenous PCM proteins in C. elegans as described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Live imaging of PCM components at the end of mitosis revealed two phases of disassembly, beginning with the gradual dissolution of PCM proteins such as PLK-1, SPD-2, TAC-1, and MZT-1, followed by the rupture of the remaining PCM proteins ZYG-9, SPD-5, γ-TuRC, TPXL-1, and AIR-1 into microtubule associated packets.
claims.source: Live imaging of PCM components at the end of mitosis revealed two phases of disassembly, beginning with the gradual dissolution of PCM proteins such as PLK-1, SPD-2, TAC-1, and MZT-1, followed by the rupture of the remaining PCM proteins ZYG-9, SPD-5, γ-TuRC, TPXL-1, and AIR-1 into microtubule associated packets.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging experiments described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Phosphatases play a role in PCM disassembly throughout mitosis, opposing CDK activity during PCM assembly and catalyzing PCM dissolution once CDK activity naturally dissipated.
claims.source: Using pharmacological and genetic perturbations, we found a role for phosphatases in PCM disassembly throughout mitosis, opposing CDK activity during PCM assembly and catalyzing PCM dissolution once CDK activity naturally dissipated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological and genetic perturbation experiments described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The nature of the remaining PCM was transformed and mechanically cleared from the centrosome by cortical pulling forces.
claims.source: Cell fusion and RNAi experiments indicated that the nature of the remaining PCM was transformed and mechanically cleared from the centrosome by cortical pulling forces.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell fusion and RNAi experiments described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Delay in PCM removal impacted subsequent centriole separation and PCM maturation in the next cell cycle.
claims.source: Delay in PCM removal impacted subsequent centriole separation and PCM maturation in the next cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The inactivation of MTOC function at the centrosome involves a regulated two-step process of PCM disassembly, the timing of which is critical to the developing embryo.
claims.source: These data indicate that the inactivation of MTOC function at the centrosome involves a regulated two-step process of PCM disassembly, the timing of which is critical to the developing embryo.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: ABp has relatively large centrosomes oriented during mitosis along the left-right axis of the embryo, with one of the centrosomes positioned very close to the coverslip in an end-on orientation.
claims.source: ABp has relatively large centrosomes oriented during mitosis along the left-right axis of the embryo, with one of the centrosomes positioned very close to the coverslip in an end-on orientation (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1A.

claims.claim: At NEBD in the ABp cell, the centrosome still functions as an MTOC, actively growing and organizing microtubules.
claims.source: At this time, the centrosome still functions as an MTOC, actively growing and organizing microtubules (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1A.

claims.claim: SAS-4 localizes at the center of the centrosome.
claims.source: As expected, the centrioles sit at the center of the centrosome (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and D) surrounded by PCM proteins which formed ordered layers of protein localization.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1B-C.

claims.claim: PCM proteins form ordered layers of protein localization surrounding the centrioles.
claims.source: As expected, the centrioles sit at the center of the centrosome (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and D) surrounded by PCM proteins which formed ordered layers of protein localization.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1B-C.

claims.claim: SPD-2 and SPD-5 localization at the PCM is co-dependent.
claims.source: SPD-2 and SPD-5 localization at the PCM is co-dependent (Hamill et al., 2002; Kemp et al., 2004; Pelletier et al., 2004), however these proteins displayed distinct outer localization boundaries within the PCM
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: SPD-2 and SPD-5 display distinct outer localization boundaries within the PCM.
claims.source: SPD-2 and SPD-5 localization at the PCM is co-dependent (Hamill et al., 2002; Kemp et al., 2004; Pelletier et al., 2004), however these proteins displayed distinct outer localization boundaries within the PCM
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Both SPD-2 and SPD-5 localize to a more proximal region surrounding the centrioles (distance from center at half maximum intensity for SPD-2: −0.575–0.575 ± 0.02 µm; 77.8 ± 0.8% of total SPD-5 overlapping with SPD-2 in this region).
claims.source: both SPD-2 and SPD-5 localized to a more proximal region surrounding the centrioles (distance from center at half maximum intensity for SPD-2: −0.575–0.575 ± 0.02 µm; 77.8 ± 0.8% of total SPD-5 overlapping with SPD-2 in this region)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data.

claims.claim: SPD-5 extends to a more distal region lacking SPD-2 (distance from center at half maximum intensity for SPD-5: −0.83–0.83 ± 0.03 µm).
claims.source: and SPD-5 extended to a more distal region lacking SPD-2 (distance from center at half maximum intensity for SPD-5: −0.83–0.83 ± 0.03 µm; Figure 1B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data and Figure 1B-C.

claims.claim: The PCM is divided into an 'inner' and 'outer' sphere, with the smaller inner sphere defined by the outer edge of SPD-2 localization and the larger outer sphere defined by the outer edge of SPD-5 localization.
claims.source: Based on the outer edge of these two matrix proteins, we divide the PCM into an 'inner' and 'outer' sphere, with the smaller inner sphere defined by the outer edge of SPD-2 localization and the larger outer sphere defined by the outer edge of SPD-5 localization (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and analysis described in the manuscript and Figure 1D.

claims.claim: PLK-1 shows the most restricted localization, occupying a relatively proximal localization in the inner sphere.
claims.source: PLK-1 showed the most restricted localization, occupying a relatively proximal localization in the inner sphere (Figure 1B,C,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1B,C,E.

claims.claim: GIP-1 localization is indistinguishable from SPD-5, extending into the outer sphere.
claims.source: GIP-1 localization was indistinguishable from SPD-5, extending into the outer sphere (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and D)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1B-C.

claims.claim: MZT-1 shows an intermediary localization, extending only partially into the outer sphere.
claims.source: however another γ-TuRC component MZT-1 showed an intermediary localization, extending only partially into the outer sphere (Figure 1B–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1B-C.

claims.claim: TAC-1 and ZYG-9 share an intermediate localization pattern.
claims.source: TAC-1 and ZYG-9 also shared this intermediate localization pattern (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1C.

claims.claim: AIR-1 localization is mainly restricted to the outer sphere, forming a toroid as previously reported.
claims.source: Finally, the localization of AIR-1 was mainly restricted to the outer sphere, forming a toroid as previously reported (Hannak et al., 2001) and a complimentary localization pattern to PLK-1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: TPXL-1 and AIR-1 co-localize, consistent with the fact that TPXL-1 is important for AIR-1 recruitment to the centrosome and microtubules.
claims.source: As expected, TPXL-1 and AIR-1 co-localized, consistent with the fact that TPXL-1 is important for AIR-1 recruitment to the centrosome and microtubules (Toya et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Both TPXL-1 and AIR-1 localization extend further than the boundary of SPD-5 and GIP-1.
claims.source: Both TPXL-1 and AIR-1 localization extended further than the boundary of SPD-5 and GIP-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D.

claims.claim: The PCM has a layered structure with an inner sphere delimited by SPD-2 localization that also localizes SPD-5, PLK-1, ZYG-9, TAC-1, γ-TuRC components, AIR-1, and TPXL-1.
claims.source: Based on these observations, we conclude that the PCM has a layered structure with an inner sphere delimited by SPD-2 localization (Figure 1D) that also localizes SPD-5, PLK-1, ZYG-9, TAC-1, γ-TuRC components, AIR-1, and TPXL-1
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and analysis described in the manuscript and Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The PCM has an outer sphere delimited by SPD-5 localization that also contains ZYG-9, TAC-1, GIP-1, MZT-1, AIR-1, and TPXL-1.
claims.source: and an outer sphere delimited by SPD-5 localization that also contains ZYG-9, TAC-1, GIP-1, MZT-1, AIR-`1, and TPXL-1 (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and analysis described in the manuscript and Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The boundaries of PCM protein localization follow the general pattern of the predicted orthologs in Drosophila and human cells.
claims.source: Although our imaging approach did not allow us to resolve toroidal localization patterns of the majority of the PCM proteins we analyzed, the boundaries of PCM protein localization follows the general pattern of the predicted orthologs in Drosophila and human cells (Fu and Glover, 2012; Lawo et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to previous studies cited.

claims.claim: SPD-5 and GIP-1 are found in a region lacking known binding partners SPD-2 and MZT-1, respectively.
claims.source: This localization pattern is also noteworthy as SPD-5 and GIP-1 are found in a region lacking known binding partners SPD-2 and MZT-1, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: SPD-2, MZT-1, TAC-1, and PLK-1 display similar disassembly behaviors, leaving the centrosome by gradual 'dissolution' over time and eventually only remaining at the two centrioles that will duplicate and mature into new centrosomes.
claims.source: SPD-2 (Video 1), MZT-1 (Video 2), TAC-1, and PLK-1 displayed similar disassembly behaviors, leaving the centrosome by gradual 'dissolution' over time and eventually only remaining at the two centrioles that will duplicate and mature into new centrosomes (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging experiments described in the manuscript and Figure 1E.

claims.claim: SPD-5, GIP-1, ZYG-9, AIR-1, and TPXL-1 initially show some gradual disassembly, however the structure containing these proteins then appears to 'rupture' and fragment into 'packets' that are distinct from the centrioles.
claims.source: In contrast, SPD-5 (Video 3), GIP-1 (Video 4), ZYG-9, AIR-1, and TPXL-1 initially showed some gradual disassembly, however the structure containing these proteins then appeared to 'rupture' and fragment into 'packets' that were distinct from the centrioles (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging experiments described in the manuscript and Figure 2A-C.

claims.claim: Sub-PCM packets localize SPD-5, GIP-1, microtubules, AIR-1, and TPXL-1, but neither SPD-2 nor MZT-1.
claims.source: These sub-PCM packets localized SPD-5, GIP-1 (Figure 2A, early packets), microtubules (Figure 2B, early packets), AIR-1 (Figure 2C, early packets), and TPXL-1, but neither SPD-2 nor MZT-1 (Figure 2E, see below).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 2A-C, 2E.

claims.claim: Packets appear to retain MTOC potential as EBP-2/EB1 comets, a marker of growing microtubule plus ends, dynamically move from the SPD-5/GIP-1 foci.
claims.source: Intriguingly, packets appeared to retain MTOC potential as EBP-2/EB1 comets, a marker of growing microtubule plus ends, dynamically moved from the SPD-5/GIP-1 foci (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Packets are further disassembled in the cytoplasm following their removal from the PCM, with GIP-1 and microtubules first losing their association, followed by SPD-5.
claims.source: The packets appeared to be further disassembled in the cytoplasm following their removal from the PCM, with GIP-1 and microtubules first losing their association, followed by SPD-5 (Figure 2A–C, late packets, Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 2A-C, 2F.

claims.claim: SPD-2 shows a gradual decrease in intensity beginning at 2 min post-NEBD (2.20 ± 0.13 min, n = 10).
claims.source: SPD-2 (Figure 3A) and MZT-1 (Figure 3B) showed a gradual decrease in intensity, beginning at 2 (2.20 ± 0.13 min, n = 10) or 3 min (3.00 ± 0.27 min, n = 8) post-NEBD, respectively
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data and Figure 3A.

claims.claim: MZT-1 shows a gradual decrease in intensity beginning at 3 min post-NEBD (3.00 ± 0.27 min, n = 8).
claims.source: SPD-2 (Figure 3A) and MZT-1 (Figure 3B) showed a gradual decrease in intensity, beginning at 2 (2.20 ± 0.13 min, n = 10) or 3 min (3.00 ± 0.27 min, n = 8) post-NEBD, respectively
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data and Figure 3B.

claims.claim: SPD-2 and MZT-1 show a decrease in PCM volume beginning 3 min post-NEBD (SPD-2: 3.00 ± 0.21 min, n = 10; MZT-1: 2.88 ± 0.23 min, n = 8).
claims.source: and a decrease in PCM volume beginning 3 min post-NEBD (SPD-2: 3.00 ± 0.21 min, n = 10; MZT-1: 2.88 ± 0.23 min, n = 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data.

claims.claim: SPD-2 and MZT-1 changes occur several minutes before the decrease in either SPD-5 or GIP-1.
claims.source: These changes occurred several minutes before the decrease in either SPD-5 or GIP-1 (Figure 3D–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data and Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: PLK-1 and TAC-1 show a similar disassembly behavior as SPD-2 and MZT-1, with a gradual decrease in intensity beginning at 2 min post-NEBD (n = 7).
claims.source: PLK-1 and TAC-1 showed a similar disassembly behavior as SPD-2 and MZT-1, with a gradual decrease in intensity beginning at 2 min post-NEBD (n = 7, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Both SPD-5 and GIP-1 colocalize during the process of disassembly.
claims.source: As expected from our observation of their individual localization behaviors, both SPD-5 and GIP-1 colocalized during the process of disassembly (Figure 3C, Video 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 3C, Video 5.

claims.claim: Both SPD-5 and GIP-1 begin a rapid decrease in intensity following their peak at 3 min post-NEBD (SPD-5: 3.00 ± 0.14 min, n = 11; GIP-1: 3.18 ± 0.12 min, n = 11).
claims.source: Both proteins began a rapid decrease in intensity following their peak at 3 min post-NEBD (SPD-5: 3.00 ± 0.14 min, n = 11; GIP-1: 3.18 ± 0.12 min, n = 11; Figure 3D–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data and Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: SPD-5 and GIP-1 volume remains unchanged until 6 min post-NEBD (SPD-5: 5.91 ± 0.17 min, n = 11; GIP-1: 6.00 ± 0.19 min, n = 11), at which time changes in the structural integrity of the PCM as holes appear.
claims.source: Their volume, however, remained unchanged until 6 min post-NEBD (SPD-5: 5.91 ± 0.17 min, n = 11; GIP-1: 6.00 ± 0.19 min, n = 11), at which time we began to see changes in the structural integrity of the PCM as holes appeared.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data.

claims.claim: The appearance of holes in the PCM and the concomitant change in PCM volume is referred to as 'rupture'.
claims.source: We refer to the appearance of these holes and the concomitant change in PCM volume as 'rupture'.
claims.evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors based on their observations.

claims.claim: Following rupture, SPD-5 and GIP-1 deformation continues until distinct sub-PCM 'packets' can be observed individualized from the two future centrosomes.
claims.source: Following rupture, SPD-5 and GIP-1 deformation continued until distinct sub-PCM 'packets' could be observed individualized from the two future centrosomes (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Both AIR-1 and TPXL-1 appear to spread onto the microtubules starting 3 min post-NEBD, 3 min ahead of SPD-5 and GIP-1 rupture, before also localizing in packets.
claims.source: Intriguingly, both AIR-1 and TPXL-1 appeared to spread onto the microtubules starting 3 min post-NEBD (Figure 2C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), 3 min ahead of SPD-5 and GIP-1 rupture, before also localizing in packets.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 2C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The PCM disassembles in two distinct steps: a dissolution step characterized by the decrease in intensity of PCM proteins that starts with the removal of the most internal proteins, PLK-1, SPD-2, TAC-1 and MZT-1; and a rupture step where the deformation and subsequent separation of the PCM leads to further disassembly into individual packets.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that the PCM disassembles in two distinct steps: a dissolution step that is characterized by the decrease in intensity of PCM proteins that starts with the removal of the most internal proteins, PLK-1, SPD-2, TAC-1 and MZT-1; and a rupture step where the deformation and subsequent separation of the PCM leads to further disassembly into individual packets.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and analysis described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The formation of packets that appear to be pulled away from the centrioles suggests that mechanical forces underlie this aspect of PCM disassembly.
claims.source: The formation of packets that appear to be pulled away from the centrioles suggests that mechanical forces underlie this aspect of PCM disassembly.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claims.claim: Forces can be exerted on the PCM by a conserved cortically anchored complex of LIN-5/NuMA, (GPR-1/2)/LGN, and (GOA-1/GPA-16)/Gαi, which localizes dynein-dynactin and can pull on the astral microtubules extending from the PCM.
claims.source: Forces can be exerted on the PCM by a conserved cortically anchored complex of LIN-5/NuMA, (GPR-1/2)/LGN, and (GOA-1/GPA-16)/Gαi, which localizes dynein-dynactin and can pull on the astral microtubules extending from the PCM (Kotak and Gönczy, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Greater cortical forces exist in the posterior of the one-cell C. elegans embryo.
claims.source: Given that greater cortical forces exist in the posterior of the one-cell C. elegans embryo, it has been hypothesized that these forces could be responsible for the asynchrony observed in the disassembly of the anterior vs. the posterior centrosome (Grill et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: It has been hypothesized that cortical forces could be responsible for the asynchrony observed in the disassembly of the anterior vs. the posterior centrosome.
claims.source: Given that greater cortical forces exist in the posterior of the one-cell C. elegans embryo, it has been hypothesized that these forces could be responsible for the asynchrony observed in the disassembly of the anterior vs. the posterior centrosome (Grill et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on a hypothesis from a previous study cited.

claims.claim: A recent study implicated the (GPR-1/2)/LIN-5/DHC-1 complex in SPD-5 disassembly from the PCM.
claims.source: Moreover, a recent study implicated the (GPR-1/2)/LIN-5/DHC-1 complex in SPD-5 disassembly from the PCM (Enos et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: In control embryos treated with lacZ RNAi, SPD-5 ruptured starting 6 min post-NEBD (5.91 ± 0.16 min, n = 11).
claims.source: In control embryos treated with lacZ RNAi, SPD-5 ruptured starting 6 min post-NEBD (5.91 ± 0.16 min, n = 11; Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data and Figure 4A.

claims.claim: SPD-5 rupture or packet formation was not observed in gpr-1/2(RNAi) treated embryos.
claims.source: In contrast, we did not observe SPD-5 rupture or packet formation in gpr-1/2(RNAi) treated embryos (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In gpr-1/2(RNAi) treated embryos, SPD-5 disassembles by gradual dissolution as indicated by the steady decrease in SPD-5 centrosomal volume which is in sharp contrast to the precipitous drop off seen in control embryos.
claims.source: Instead, SPD-5, like SPD-2, disassembled by gradual dissolution as indicated by the steady decrease in SPD-5 centrosomal volume which was in sharp contrast to the precipitous drop off seen in control embryos (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In csnk-1(RNAi) treated embryos, slightly earlier SPD-5 rupture was observed (5.4 + 0.2 min, n = 7).
claims.source: In csnk-1(RNAi) treated embryos, we observed slightly earlier SPD-5 rupture (5.4 + 0.2 min, n = 7; Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data and Figure 4A.

claims.claim: SPD-2 disassembly is unaffected following depletion of either gpr-1/2 or csnk-1 by RNAi.
claims.source: In contrast to SPD-5, SPD-2 disassembly was unaffected following depletion of either gpr-1/2 or csnk-1 by RNAi (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 4C.

claims.claim: SPD-5 levels at the PCM are increased by gpr-1/2 and decreased by csnk-1 depletion.
claims.source: Interestingly, SPD-5 levels at the PCM were increased by gpr-1/2 and decreased by csnk-1 depletion (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Cortical forces generate the mechanical forces necessary for rupture and packet formation, allowing for the efficient removal of the outer sphere protein SPD-5 but not the exclusively inner sphere protein SPD-2.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that cortical forces generate the mechanical forces necessary for rupture and packet formation, allowing for the efficient removal of the outer sphere protein SPD-5 but not the exclusively inner sphere protein SPD-2.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Astral microtubules show a striking network reorganization post-NEBD, growing progressively longer and contacting the cell cortex, sometimes wrapping around the membrane prior to rupture and packet formation.
claims.source: Astral microtubules showed a striking network reorganization post-NEBD, growing progressively longer and contacting the cell cortex, sometimes wrapping around the membrane prior to rupture and packet formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: A similar reorganization of AIR-1 and TPXL-1 was observed, which coat astral microtubules.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: No change in the gross cortical distribution or intensity of LIN-5, DNC-1, or DHC-1 was observed post-NEBD.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D.

claims.claim: An ephemeral redistribution of DHC-1 coincident with rupture was observed.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed an ephemeral redistribution of DHC-1 coincident with rupture (Figure 4—figure supplements 2E and 4 min.).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: Although cortical complexes are present throughout the cell cycle, they may only make productive contact with astral microtubules at a particular time period to allow for outer sphere disassembly.
claims.source: This pattern of localization suggests that although cortical complexes are present throughout the cell cycle, they may only make productive contact with astral microtubules at a particular time period to allow for outer sphere disassembly.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claims.claim: In control embryos, the centriolar pair appears as a single SAS-4 focus up to 5 min post-NEBD.
claims.source: In control embryos, the centriolar pair appeared as a single SAS-4 focus up to 5 min post-NEBD (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Two closely apposed SAS-4 foci become apparent beginning at 5 min post-NEBD (Stage 1), which quickly separate by greater than 1 µm beginning about 1 min later (Stage 2).
claims.source: Two closely apposed SAS-4 foci became apparent beginning at 5 min post-NEBD (Stage 1, Figure 4D), which quickly separated by greater than 1 µm beginning about 1 min later (Stage 2, Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and Figure 4D.

claims.claim: A significant delay in the onsets of both Stage one and Stage two centriole separation was observed in gpr-1/2(RNAi) treated embryos, but no significant change in csnk-1(RNAi) treated embryos.
claims.source: We saw a significant delay in the onsets of both Stage one and Stage two in gpr-1/2(RNAi) treated embryos, but no significant change in csnk-1(RNAi) treated embryos (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data and Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Cortical forces facilitate centriole separation either through direct force transmission or indirectly through their role in PCM removal.
claims.source: These results suggest that cortical forces facilitate centriole separation either through direct force transmission or indirectly through their role in PCM removal.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claims.claim: A force-independent licensing event is necessary to initiate centriole separation.
claims.source: That csnk-1 RNAi had no effect on the timing of centriole separation suggests that a force-independent licensing event is necessary to initiate separation (Cabral et al., 2013; Tsou and Stearns, 2006), but that centrioles are subsequently held together by PCM.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Centrioles are held together by PCM.

results.result: The C. elegans PCM is organized into discrete inner and outer spheres with distinct protein localization patterns. The inner sphere is delimited by SPD-2 localization and the outer sphere by SPD-5 localization, with various PCM proteins (PLK-1, MZT-1, TAC-1, ZYG-9, GIP-1, AIR-1, TPXL-1) showing differential localization across these spheres. This layered organization appears conserved with Drosophila and human PCM.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C41-C67, C156-C158 collectively demonstrate the spatial organization of the PCM through quantitative imaging of endogenously-tagged proteins. The measurements of protein localization boundaries (half-maximum intensity distances) and the observation that known binding partners (SPD-5/SPD-2, GIP-1/MZT-1) occupy distinct regions provide strong evidence for the two-sphere model. The comparison to other organisms (C66, C157) is appropriately cited.

results.result: PCM disassembly occurs through two distinct sequential steps: (1) dissolution, characterized by gradual decrease in intensity of inner sphere proteins (PLK-1, SPD-2, TAC-1, MZT-1) beginning 2-3 min post-NEBD, and (2) rupture, where outer sphere proteins (SPD-5, GIP-1, ZYG-9, AIR-1, TPXL-1) fragment into packets beginning ~6 min post-NEBD. These packets retain MTOC potential and undergo further disassembly in the cytoplasm.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C68-C84, C162 are well-supported by live imaging time-course data with quantitative measurements of intensity and volume changes. The temporal sequence is clearly documented with specific timepoints and sample sizes (n=7-11). The observation that packets retain MTOC potential (C71) is supported by EBP-2 comet tracking. The correlation between protein localization patterns and disassembly modes strengthens the two-sphere model.

results.result: Cortical pulling forces mediate PCM rupture and packet formation specifically for outer sphere proteins. RNAi depletion of gpr-1/2 eliminates SPD-5 rupture/packet formation while leaving SPD-2 dissolution unaffected. Cortical forces also tune SPD-5 levels at the PCM and facilitate centriole separation. The effect of cortical forces is temporally restricted, with PCM becoming sensitive to these forces in late anaphase coincident with microtubule network reorganization.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C105, C213-C216 are supported by RNAi experiments showing differential effects on SPD-5 vs SPD-2 (C91-C94), quantitative volume measurements (C92), and centriole separation timing (C104). The temporal restriction is supported by microtubule reorganization observations (C97) and FP treatment experiments showing dissolution rather than rupture when PCM is precociously removed (C217). However, the mechanism by which cortical forces specifically affect outer sphere proteins could benefit from additional mechanistic detail.

results.result: PP2A phosphatases, particularly LET-92, control PCM dissolution by opposing kinase activity throughout mitosis. Pharmacological inhibition (okadaic acid, rubratoxin A) and let-92 RNAi stabilize PCM at the centrosome and impair dissolution of both SPD-2 and SPD-5. Combined inhibition of let-92 and gpr-1/2 completely blocks PCM removal, demonstrating that both phosphatase activity and cortical forces are required for efficient PCM disassembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C44, C111-C126, C152, C165-C168 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: pharmacological inhibition experiments (C112-C113), genetic perturbations (C114-C122), and localization studies showing LET-92 at the centrosome throughout mitosis (C124-C126). The double perturbation experiment (C122) provides strong evidence for the requirement of both mechanisms. However, whether LET-92 acts directly on PCM proteins or indirectly through kinases remains unresolved (C169), which is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Phosphatases actively oppose PCM assembly throughout mitosis, creating a balance with kinase activity. CDK inhibition (flavopiridol) causes precocious PCM disassembly that is blocked by co-treatment with okadaic acid, demonstrating continuous phosphatase opposition. SPD-2 and SPD-5 show differential regulation, with SPD-2 being positively regulated by an OA-sensitive phosphatase distinct from LET-92.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C138, C170-C178 are supported by timed drug treatment experiments showing stage-specific effects of FP and OA. The observation that FP+OA stabilizes SPD-5 but not SPD-2 (C135-C136) provides evidence for differential regulation. The model that phosphatases continuously oppose assembly (C133, C170, C172) is well-supported by the immediate disassembly upon CDK inhibition. The speculation about mechanisms (C173, C175-C176) is appropriately identified as such.

results.result: Assembling and disassembling PCM are mutually resistant states that cannot be interconverted by cytoplasmic factors. Cell fusion experiments show that disassembling PCM continues to form packets despite exposure to assembly-competent cytoplasm, and assembling PCM is unaffected by disassembly-competent cytoplasm. New PCM assembly only occurs after old PCM is completely removed. This suggests the PCM undergoes a structural transformation during mitosis, possibly from liquid-like to gel-like properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C150, C184-C194 are supported by cell fusion experiments (C141-C146) showing that neither assembling nor disassembling PCM is affected by the opposing cytoplasmic environment. The observation that new PCM only assembles after old PCM removal (C144, C148) is clearly documented. The speculation about biophysical changes (C189-C194) is appropriately identified and supported by citations to in vitro studies (C190). However, the molecular basis for this resistance remains unclear and would benefit from further investigation.

results.result: Timely PCM removal is critical for subsequent cell cycle events. Delayed PCM removal following gpr-1/2 RNAi impairs centriole separation and delays subsequent SPD-5 accumulation in the next cell cycle. Centriole separation requires both a force-independent licensing event and subsequent PCM removal by cortical forces.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47, C104-C110 are supported by quantitative measurements showing delayed centriole separation (C104) and SPD-5 accumulation (C109) following gpr-1/2 RNAi. The observation that csnk-1 RNAi does not affect centriole separation timing (C104) supports the licensing model (C106). However, the mechanism by which PCM holds centrioles together (C107) is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: SPD-2 association with the centrosome is positively regulated by an OA-sensitive phosphatase distinct from LET-92, further separating SPD-2 regulation from SPD-5. OA treatment causes precocious SPD-2 disassembly only after NEBD, suggesting temporal/spatial regulation of this phosphatase. PP1 and/or PP4 are candidate phosphatases for this role.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C183 are supported by the differential effects of OA vs let-92 RNAi on SPD-2 (C179). The temporal specificity (C181) is clearly documented. However, the identification of PP1/PP4 as candidates (C182) is speculative and based only on literature precedent, not direct experimental evidence in this study. This represents a testable hypothesis for future work.

results.result: Phosphorylation may regulate PCM structural properties. let-92 depletion inhibits rupture and produces more fluid packets, consistent with phosphorylation affecting PCM material properties. Complementary localization of PLK-1 and AIR-1 could create different phosphorylation landscapes, with AIR-1 potentially active throughout the outer sphere via TPXL-1 interaction.
results.evaluation: Claim C195 is supported by experimental observations of altered packet properties following let-92 depletion. However, claims C197-C201 are largely speculative. The role of PCMD-1 (C197) is based only on comparison to another study. The model of differential phosphorylation landscapes (C198, C201) and AIR-1 activation throughout the outer sphere (C200-C201) are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support in this study. These represent interesting directions for future investigation.

results.result: PCM packets retain MTOC potential and are reminiscent of PCM flares in Drosophila and centrosome fragments in LLC-PK1 cells, suggesting conservation of PCM fragmentation mechanisms. Packets disassemble through kinase/phosphatase-independent mechanisms, possibly involving rapid diffusion or proteasome-based degradation.
results.evaluation: Claim C202 is well-supported by EBP-2 comet tracking data. The comparison to flares and fragments (C203-C210) is reasonable but reveals both similarities and differences in molecular composition (C207-C208), making the degree of conservation unclear. The mechanism of packet disassembly (C211-C212) is entirely speculative with no experimental evidence provided. This would require additional investigation to determine the actual mechanisms involved.

results.result: The effect of cortical forces on PCM is temporally restricted to late anaphase. When PCM is precociously removed by FP treatment, it disassembles by dissolution rather than rupture. Astral microtubule reorganization beginning in anaphase increases cortex contact. AIR-1 and TPXL-1 spread along microtubules starting at the end of anaphase, potentially contributing to microtubule reorganization.
results.evaluation: Claims C217-C221 are supported by experimental observations: FP treatment causes dissolution (C217), microtubule reorganization is documented (C218), and AIR-1/TPXL-1 spreading is observed (C221). The temporal correlation supports the model that cortical forces only act productively in late anaphase (C219). However, the functional significance of AIR-1/TPXL-1 redistribution (C222-C223) is speculative. The slight effect of CSNK-1 inhibition (C220) is consistent with the model but suggests additional complexity.

results.result: Summary claims stating the main conclusions: MTOC inactivation involves two-step PCM disassembly (dissolution then rupture), cortical forces drive rupture, and PCM is a complex meshwork with distinct regulatory mechanisms rather than a uniformly regulated mass.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C155 represent summary statements of the major findings that are well-supported by the collective evidence from the grouped results above. These integrate the spatial organization, temporal dynamics, and regulatory mechanisms into a coherent model.

results.result: Inner sphere proteins (SPD-2, MZT-1) disassemble before outer sphere proteins (SPD-5, GIP-1), and SPD-5/GIP-1 can form a matrix in the absence of SPD-2/MZT-1. Differences in disassembly behaviors may reflect differences in protein mobility within the PCM, with more fluid inner sphere proteins relying on active turnover while stable outer sphere proteins require physical disruption.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C160 are directly supported by the temporal measurements and OA treatment experiments. Claim C161 about SPD-5 matrix formation is appropriately cited. Claims C163-C164 represent reasonable inferences based on published mobility data (C163 is cited) and the observed disassembly behaviors, though the mechanistic link between mobility and disassembly mode is not directly tested.
